catalog_quote: p.160: "Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date." p.152: "Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. ... All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent. The remainder of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi (Kim 1995) and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise (Clouse n.d.1)."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kirikiri (a western Tariku / Lakes Plain language) is tonal, with high, low, falling and rising tones (Clouse 2002 counts six phonemic tone patterns); stress has not been found to be contrastive in any Lakes Plain language, and no source states a position for word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the stress remark is a blanket statement about the Lakes Plain family based on the author's own Kirikiri fieldwork (1989-1992) and the other SIL phonologies; the tone remark cites Heljä Clouse's unpublished 'An autosegmental approach to Kirikiri tone (notes)'.
new_statements.domain_note: Comparative 267-item word lists (citation forms); statement is family-level (all Lakes Plain languages), not a Kirikiri-specific phonology section.
new_statements.identity_note: Clouse 1997's stress remark is family-level ("any of the Lakes Plain languages") but comes from the Kirikiri fieldworker (D. & H. Clouse, Wahuka, 1989-1992), and the tone remark applies to Kirikiri as a western Tariku language (via Heljä Clouse's unpublished Kirikiri tone notes). Kirikiri has three dialect groups Kirikiri, Taû and Faia (Glottolog: Nuclear Kirikiri nucl1599, Faia faia1238; Faia 89% cognate per Clouse 1997: 148); the Clouse data are from the Kirikiri (Wahuka) dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Yoder, Brendon E. 2020. A grammar of Abawiri, a Lakes Plain language of Papua, Indonesia. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara. xxix+600 pp. (eScholarship item 4mj571tr).
tone_statements.quote: In Kirikiri, two level tones, /L/ and /H/, combine into seven tone patterns on nouns. Lexical tone contrast on verbs is less clear because of final pitch declination (verbs occur clause-finally). Some TAM suffixes bear tone; further, a few aspectual distinctions are coded by tone alone (Clouse n.d.).
tone_statements.locator: p.66, ch. 2 sec. 2.4 'Tone', survey paragraph 'There are basic descriptions of at least seven other Lakes Plain tone systems'; also p.13 and reference list p.585.
tone_statements.summary: Two underlying level tones (L, H) yielding seven lexical tone patterns on nouns; verb tone partly grammatical (tonal TAM suffixes, aspect by tone alone), surface verb contrasts blurred by clause-final declination.
